purpose: Describe coherent biblical situations once so comparator relations can point to whole scenes instead of repeatedly reducing stories to isolated verse fragments.

scenes.title: Jacob's ladder and the naming of Bethel
scenes.summary: Jacob, traveling away from home, sleeps in the open and dreams of a stairway joining earth and heaven with divine messengers ascending and descending. He wakes in awe, calls the place God's house and the gate of heaven, and marks the place with a stone.
scenes.setting: Jacob's journey from Beersheba toward Haran; an unnamed stopping place later called Bethel
scenes.lead_in: Jacob has left his family after the conflict around Isaac's blessing and is traveling toward his mother's relatives.
scenes.outcome: A vulnerable roadside stop is reinterpreted as a sacred meeting-place joining earth, heaven, house and gate imagery.
scenes.what_follows: Jacob continues toward Haran; the Bethel encounter remains important in his later return narrative.
scenes.historical_context: The scene belongs to the patriarchal Jacob cycle and functions as a place-founding and promise-renewal narrative.
scenes.literary_context: Genesis 28 follows Jacob's departure and extends the ancestral promises into his exile/journey.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: English translations vary between ladder and stairway; the Hebrew term denotes a structure set on earth with its top toward heaven.
counterreadings_or_limits: The scene does not identify Jacob himself as the stairway.

scenes.title: The Son of Man becomes the locus of ascent and descent
scenes.summary: During the calling of Philip and Nathanael, Jesus promises a greater vision: heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man, deliberately echoing Jacob's stairway scene.
scenes.setting: early disciple-calling sequence in John's Gospel
scenes.lead_in: Nathanael moves from skepticism about Nazareth to recognizing Jesus after an encounter centered on being seen and known.
scenes.outcome: Jacob's heaven-earth imagery is reworked so the Son of Man becomes the relational locus of the movement.
scenes.what_follows: John proceeds into the Cana sign narrative and further identity disclosures.
scenes.historical_context: The saying participates in early Jewish scriptural reuse and Johannine identity language around Jesus.
scenes.literary_context: The Gospel opens by accumulating titles and recognitions around Jesus; this saying links that identity to Genesis 28.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The relationship to Genesis 28 is an intertextual reuse, not a repetition of Jacob's dream setting.
counterreadings_or_limits: The text does not split the passage function into a separate Father-Ladder and Son-Door architecture.

scenes.title: Door, shepherd, recognition, pasture and laying down life
scenes.summary: Jesus contrasts unauthorized entry with legitimate access, identifies himself with the sheep-door and then with the good shepherd, joining recognition, entry and exit, pasture, abundant life, protection and voluntary laying down of life.
scenes.setting: Jerusalem discourse context following the healing and exclusion conflict of John 9
scenes.lead_in: John 9 centers sight, recognition, exclusion from community and conflict with authorities; John 10 continues with images of access and legitimate care.
sequence: shepherd lays down life for sheep
scenes.outcome: Door and Shepherd become complementary access-and-care functions centered on life rather than extraction.
scenes.what_follows: The audience divides over Jesus' words; later in the chapter identity and authority disputes intensify.
scenes.historical_context: Shepherd language draws on pastoral reality and Israel's scriptural tradition of rulers and God as shepherd.
scenes.literary_context: John places this discourse immediately after a conflict over sight and exclusion, making recognition and legitimate belonging central to the imagery.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Some English versions use gate where others use door; both preserve the access-control metaphor.
counterreadings_or_limits: The discourse does not make every threshold, anatomical structure or modern interface identical to Jesus.

scenes.title: Father's House, many dwellings, Thomas' question and the Way
scenes.summary: Jesus comforts the disciples with Father's-House and dwelling imagery, speaks of preparing a place and returning, and answers Thomas' question about the way by identifying himself as the way to the Father. The scene continues into Father/Son relation and the promise not to leave the disciples orphaned.
scenes.setting: Jesus' farewell discourse before the Passion
scenes.lead_in: The meal and departure crisis has begun; betrayal and Peter's denial have been announced, creating fear around separation and where Jesus is going.
sequence: promise not to leave disciples orphaned
scenes.outcome: House, dwelling, departure, return, Way, Father and Son are joined in one separation-and-access discourse.
scenes.what_follows: John 14 continues with Spirit/Paraclete and peace language before the vine discourse of John 15.
scenes.historical_context: The discourse belongs to John's theological presentation of Jesus' impending death/departure and continuing relation to disciples.
scenes.literary_context: The scene interprets separation before the Passion through dwelling/access language rather than treating the House as a simple physical building description.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: John 14:2 is translated as rooms, dwelling places or mansions in different English traditions; the underlying image is enduring place in the Father's House.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage identifies Jesus as the Way to the Father; it does not directly identify another modern person as the Father's House.
